newsitem.title: CONGO: Mediator calls Congo Brazzaville foes to talks.
newsitem.headline: Mediator calls Congo Brazzaville foes to talks.

text.p: The national mediation committee trying to end warfare in the Congo Republic capital on Sunday called the protagonists to the first direct talks.
The latest ceasefire in the month-long tribal and political conflict in Brazzaville appeared to be holding despite a burst of mortar fire earlier in the day, residents said.

"The national mediation committee urges the conflicting parties to take part in political talks starting on Wednesday July 9 in Brazzaville," the committee said in a statement signed by its chairman Bernard Kolelas, the city mayor.
Kolelas read the statement to reporters but declined to give details about the talks before Wednesday or to answer questions.

It was not clear if the two parties -- forces supporting President Pascal Lissouba and militia fighters loyal to his predecessor and rival, Denis Sassou Nguesso, had agreed to take part in the talks and at what level.
Kolelas has met Lissouba and Sassou separately.
In the same statement, the committee said it was pleased to note that both parties in the conflict had given their written acceptance of a truce.
It stressed that a permanent ceasefire entailed a halt to all fighting and a ban on stocking up on arms and munitions.
Brazzaville was calm on Sunday afternoon after some sporadic fring earlier in the day.

The conflict opposing Lissouba and Sassou, which has now entered its second month, has left hundreds of people dead, tens of thousands displaced and whole districts of the normally sleepy Congolese capital devastated.
The focus of the earlier shelling was not clear. Residents say recent firing in the city is largely by uncontrollable elements in the rival forces.
Warfare erupted on June 5 when government troops surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militias ahead of planned July 27 elections.
Ceasefires have come and gone but diplomats said Kolelas appeared to have made progress in mediation.
"Kolelas seems to be making progress with his negotiations," one diplomat told Reuters in Kinshasa, capital of Democratic Republic of the Congo across the river from Brazzaville.
But many Brazzaville residents, trapped at home by fighting and recalling shattered ceasefires, appeared less optimistic.
"There's no sign of any improvement," said a U.N. security adviser who has spent most of the past month in Brazzaville.
Efforts to resolve the conflict have been dogged by squabbling over who started the fighting.
However, the most contentious issue now is whether Lissouba's mandate should be extended by three months to allow the organisation of elections, which look certain to be delayed.

Lissouba insists he is constitutionally entitled to an extension given the prevailing conditions. Sassou favours a transitional authority to steer the former French Central African colony through elections.
Both sides appear to agree on the need to put back the elections and on the role of the mediation committee, a broad-based body on which the warring parties as well as civic groups are represented.
Supporters of Mayor Kolelas were at the centre of similar fighting in 1993 but have remained neutral this time.
Veteran President Omar Bongo of neighbouring Gabon, a son-in-law of Sassou and a friend of Lissouba, is leading a separate international mediation effort.
Ethnic and political clashes killed at least 2,000 people in Brazzaville after a disputed 1993 parliamentary election.
